title: GPT-6 enters the field without a dedicated biological model: 322 designed proteins go to the lab, about 10% show signs of binding
excerpt: Can chat-based large models do the work of specialized biological models? In a preprint released on November 24, OpenAI gives a half-affirmative answer: the GPT
content_html:
Can chat-based large models do the work of specialized biological models? In a preprint released on November 24, OpenAI gives a half-affirmative answer: the GPT-6 series can design new protein 3D structures and amino acid sequences without relying on specialized biological models, using only reasoning and general-purpose programming tools, and it has already passed multiple rounds of laboratory testing. The tests were carried out jointly by OpenAI and its partner organization Onava.

First wins computationally, then passes wet-lab experiments

Using structures designed by GPT-6.2 as blueprints, the team created 322 miniature binding proteins covering five targets. Of these, 35 (about 10.9%) showed signs of binding, with targets including PD-L1, IL-7Rα, TrkA, VEGF-A, and IL-17A. In another experiment, GPT-6.2 rewrote the sequences of the binding loops of six antibodies; 128 of 182 tested designs (70%) were still able to bind IL-4Rα. The computational contest was even more striking: the in-house model achieved a 43.7% success rate on the “motif scaffolding” task, beating the specialized model RFdiffusion’s 27.8%; its small-molecule docking accuracy was about 93%, nearly double that of DiffDock-L (50%).

The weaknesses are also obvious

OpenAI itself set the limits: GPT-6 still needs help from specialized models such as Boltz-2 and ESMFold2 when screening candidates, and it has not yet been proven that it can design proteins end to end without these helpers. The most obvious weakness is predicting a complete structure from an amino acid sequence—the in-house model’s average TM-score is only 0.38, while ESMFold2’s is as high as 0.93. In the current workflow, GPT-6.2 is responsible for designing protein shapes that bind to specific targets, while specialized models then propose amino acid sequences and help Onava select designs worth synthesizing and testing.
